insights.title: Your breakfast may be lowering how much thyroid medicine you absorb
insights.found: Food, and some supplements, reduce how much levothyroxine your body takes up when they are taken close to the tablet.
insights.why: Your breakfast is milk with protein powder, oats, banana, yogurt and berries, and you take fibre powder in milk. We don't yet know what time you take your tablet.
insights.means: If the tablet and breakfast are close together, your body may be getting less medicine some days than others - one possible reason your TSH has moved so much this year.
insights.do: Note the time you take your tablet. Take it with water 30-60 minutes before breakfast, or at bedtime, and keep fibre and protein powders away from it. Ask your doctor before changing anything.
insights.expected: A steadier TSH at your next tests is the likely result if timing was the problem. Bedtime and morning dosing work equally well in a systematic review.
insights.helps: A simple timing change could steady your thyroid results.

insights.title: Ashwagandha can change your thyroid test results
insights.found: In a randomised trial, ashwagandha lowered TSH and raised T3 and T4 in people with a mildly underactive thyroid.
insights.why: You started ashwagandha on 2 October 2026, so your October TSH was measured while you were taking it as well as your Euthyrox.
insights.means: Your next TSH will show the effect of your tablet and the ashwagandha together, which makes it harder to judge whether your dose is right.
insights.do: Tell your doctor you take it. They may suggest pausing it before your next test, or reading the result with this in mind. Long-term use is also a reason to check liver enzymes, which are in your panel.
insights.expected: A clearer reading of your thyroid dose. This evidence comes from small trials in people not on levothyroxine, so its effect alongside your tablet is less certain.
insights.helps: Telling your doctor avoids misreading your next thyroid test.

insights.title: Some of your symptoms are worth checking against your dose
insights.found: Anxiety and headaches linked to levothyroxine happen mainly when the dose is a little too high (TSH pushed low). At the right dose, trials show no difference from placebo.
insights.why: In August your TSH was 0.52 with a high T4 (13.4), and you report anxiety and headaches. Our medical references also links both symptoms to levothyroxine.
insights.means: Your dose may have been on the high side in August. Your October TSH (4.44) was in range, so this may already have settled - a timed test will tell.
insights.do: At your next test, have the blood taken in the morning before your tablet, at the same lab, with the time written down.
insights.expected: A clear answer on whether your dose is right. Fatigue, by contrast, is more often a sign of too little medicine or another cause.
insights.helps: A well-timed test shows whether your dose is right.

insights.title: Finding out why your thyroid slowed down
insights.found: Thyroid antibody tests (anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin) show whether hypothyroidism is autoimmune, the most common cause.
insights.why: Your record has no antibody result. Thyroid problems run in your family (your mother, maternal grandfather and an uncle), and our medical references shows hypothyroidism shares immune genes with diabetes, which your father has.
insights.means: Knowing the cause shapes how your thyroid is followed over time and what your family may want to know.
insights.do: This is the first test in your personalised panel.
insights.expected: A clear cause for your hypothyroidism. Nearly all autoimmune hypothyroidism is antibody-positive.
insights.helps: One test tells you whether your thyroid condition is autoimmune.

insights.title: Check your supplements for biotin before your next test
insights.found: Biotin, found in many hair, skin and nail supplements and some B-complex products, can make thyroid test results wrong.
insights.why: We don't know the exact contents of your B12 or other supplements.
insights.means: A wrong result could lead to a dose change you don't need.
insights.do: Check the labels. If any contain biotin, stop it 2-3 days before your blood test, or tell the lab.
insights.helps: Avoids a falsely abnormal thyroid result.

insights.title: Simple causes of tiredness that haven't been checked
insights.found: Low B12 is common in hypothyroidism (about 1 in 4 in a meta-analysis), and low iron, vitamin D and poor sleep cause tiredness that thyroid treatment won't fix.
insights.why: You feel tired almost every day and sleepy some days; you're vegetarian; you take B12 and D3 but have no levels on record; your skin is very dry.
insights.means: Part of your tiredness may have a simple, fixable cause.
insights.do: Your panel includes B12, vitamin D, iron studies and a full blood count. Hypothyroidism also puts you in a group where guidelines suggest a short sleep apnoea questionnaire (STOP-Bang) - it's free.
insights.expected: Either a fixable cause, or reassurance and a narrower search.
insights.helps: Checks the common, fixable causes of tiredness and dry skin.

insights.title: Your wellbeing check-in
insights.found: Women treated for hypothyroidism report anxiety and low mood more often, even when their TSH is normal.
insights.why: Your answers give a PHQ-9 score of 8-9 (mild) and a GAD-7 score of 9-10 (between mild and moderate). Stress is 4 out of 10, mostly work and relationships, alongside 70-80 hour weeks.
insights.means: What you feel is common and recognised. It is not caused by anything you did.
insights.do: Keep going with your therapist. We'll re-check with the standard questionnaires at your next assessment. If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 (US).
insights.expected: A clearer picture over time, alongside your care.
insights.helps: Gives you and your therapist a measurable starting point.

insights.title: Your lower back: what the research suggests
insights.found: In two small trials, vitamin B12 injections reduced long-term lower back pain and disability.
insights.why: You have disc compression at L4-L5 and lower back pain for over 10 years, worse when sitting without support.
insights.means: This is an option to discuss, not a treatment recommendation. Exercise already helps you.
insights.do: Bring this to your doctor alongside your imaging report, which your panel also asks for.
insights.expected: Possible less pain. The trials were small, and the injected doses differ from your daily tablet.
insights.helps: Rules out a simple contributor to back and nerve symptoms.

insights.title: Cervical screening is due every 3 years at your age
insights.found: Guidelines recommend a cervical screening test (a smear) every 3 years for women aged 21 to 29.
insights.why: You're 24, and your records don't mention a smear test. It isn't part of thyroid or back care, so it's easy to miss.
insights.means: Screening finds early cell changes years before they could become cancer, when treatment is simple.
insights.do: If you haven't had one in the last 3 years, book one with your GP or gynaecologist. It takes a few minutes.
insights.expected: Most results are normal. If not, early follow-up is very effective.
insights.helps: Catches early changes years before they could matter.

insights.title: You can still get the HPV vaccine until you turn 27
insights.found: Catch-up HPV vaccination is recommended for everyone up to age 26 who was not fully vaccinated.
insights.why: You're 24, and we don't know whether you had it.
insights.means: HPV causes most cervical cancers. The vaccine prevents the types that cause most of them.
insights.do: Check your vaccination record. If you didn't have the full course, ask your doctor about catch-up doses.
insights.expected: Strong, long-lasting protection, alongside regular screening.
insights.helps: Strong protection against most cervical cancers, while you are still eligible.

insights.title: A tetanus, diphtheria and whooping cough booster
insights.found: Adults who never had a Tdap dose should have one, then a tetanus booster every 10 years.
insights.why: Your vaccination history isn't in your records.
insights.means: It keeps protection up, and whooping cough protection matters for anyone around newborns.
insights.do: Check when your last tetanus shot was. If unsure, ask your doctor at your panel visit.
insights.expected: One injection covers you for about 10 years.
insights.helps: Ten years of protection from one injection.

insights.title: Keep exercising for your back - the type matters less than doing it
insights.found: For long-term low back pain, exercise is a recommended treatment, and no single type works clearly better than the others.
insights.why: You have had lower back pain for over 10 years, with an L4-L5 disc compression, and you told us exercise helps.
insights.means: What you're already doing is the right kind of help. Choose what you enjoy and can keep up.
insights.do: Keep your strength training and stretches. Add back-friendly breaks from sitting at work. A physiotherapist can tailor a plan for the disc.
insights.expected: Less pain and better function over months. Evidence for disc problems specifically is less direct.
insights.helps: Confirms that what you already do is the right help for your back.

insights.title: Combination thyroid medicines are not routinely better
insights.found: Adding T3 (liothyronine) or using thyroid extract has not been shown to be consistently better than levothyroxine alone.
insights.why: You're on levothyroxine and still have tiredness and dry skin, which can make other medicines sound appealing.
insights.means: The first steps are getting your tablet timing and dose right, and checking other causes of your symptoms.
insights.do: Talk to your thyroid specialist before trying anything else. Don't change medicines on your own.
insights.expected: Most people do well on levothyroxine once dose and timing are steady.
insights.helps: Saves you from switching medicines without a clear benefit.

insights.title: If your thyroid condition is autoimmune, a few related conditions are worth knowing
insights.found: Autoimmune thyroid disease is linked with coeliac disease, autoimmune gastritis and type 1 diabetes. About 5 to 7% of people with it carry a coeliac antibody.
insights.why: We don't yet know if your hypothyroidism is autoimmune. Your father has diabetes.
insights.means: These conditions can affect how well you absorb your tablet, iron and B12, and your energy.
insights.do: Your thyroid antibody test comes first. If it is positive, ask your doctor whether a coeliac antibody test makes sense.
insights.expected: Most likely nothing is found. If something is, it is very treatable and can steady your thyroid dose.
insights.helps: Knowing early can steady your dose and your energy.

insights.title: More vegetables and fruit would help your heart in the long run
insights.found: Guidelines for all adults recommend plenty of vegetables, fruit, nuts, whole grains and lean protein, and fewer sugary drinks and refined carbohydrates.
insights.why: You eat 0 to 1 servings of fruit and vegetables a day and have sugary drinks a few times a week. Your nuts and legumes are good.
insights.means: Small changes now add up over decades for your heart and blood sugar, especially with diabetes in your family.
insights.do: Aim for a vegetable at lunch and dinner and a fruit a day. Swap sugary drinks for water most days.
insights.expected: This is general heart-health advice, not specific to thyroid. Effects build over years.
insights.helps: Small changes now protect your heart and blood sugar for decades.

insights.title: A steadier bedtime may help your energy
insights.found: Studies link poorer or shorter sleep with an underactive thyroid. Which causes which is not known.
insights.why: Your bedtime moves between 22:30 and 01:00, and you sleep badly about one night a week. You told us tiredness is worse after poor sleep.
insights.means: Regular sleep is one of the easiest levers on your daytime tiredness.
insights.do: Try to keep bedtime within the same hour most nights for a month, and note how you feel.
insights.expected: An association, not proof. It is low-risk and worth trying.
insights.helps: A free, low-risk lever on your daytime energy.

insights.title: If you ever plan a pregnancy, plan your thyroid too
insights.found: Major guidelines agree an underactive thyroid should be well controlled before conception as well as during pregnancy.
insights.why: You have treated hypothyroidism. We don't know your plans, and this only matters if and when you are thinking about it.
insights.means: Thyroid needs usually rise early in pregnancy, so doctors plan the dose ahead.
insights.do: If pregnancy is ever on your mind, tell your thyroid specialist before trying. Nothing to do now.
insights.expected: With planning, outcomes are very good.
insights.helps: With planning, outcomes are very good.

insights.title: For people of Asian heritage, health checks start at a lower BMI
insights.found: A WHO consultation set 23 as a public-health action point for body mass index in Asian populations. It is not a diagnosis.
insights.why: Your body mass index from your height and weight is at or above 23.
insights.means: It doesn't mean anything is wrong. It is a reason to measure waist, blood pressure, sugar and cholesterol, which your panel does.
insights.do: Nothing extra beyond your panel and your current exercise.
insights.expected: Your panel results will show whether this matters for you.
insights.helps: A reason to measure, not a diagnosis; your panel answers it.

ask.q: Why was my TSH so high in February?
ask.a: Your TSH was 34.37 in February, ten months after starting Euthyrox. Common reasons are the tablet being taken close to food or supplements, missed doses, or a dose that was too low at the time. It came into range by October. A timed, same-lab test will help your doctor see where things stand now.

Your latest TSH (4.44 in October) is in range. In August it was low with a high T4, which can mean a little too much. Ashwagandha may also be affecting your results. Your doctor decides the dose; a morning test before your tablet, at the same lab, gives them the clearest answer.

ask.q: When should I take my thyroid tablet?
ask.a: With water, 30-60 minutes before breakfast, or at bedtime at least 3 hours after eating. Keep fibre powder, protein powder, milk, calcium and iron away from it. A systematic review found morning and bedtime equally effective. Check with your doctor before changing.

ask.q: Could my supplements affect my thyroid?
ask.a: Yes, three ways: ashwagandha can lower TSH; fibre and protein powders near your tablet can reduce absorption; and biotin, if any product contains it, can make test results wrong. Tell your doctor about all of them.

ask.q: Why am I tired all the time?
ask.a: Tiredness with hypothyroidism is more often a sign of too little medicine or another cause than a side effect. Low B12, iron or vitamin D and poor sleep are common, fixable causes - none of them has been measured yet. Your panel covers them, plus a free sleep questionnaire.

ask.q: Could my headaches or anxiety come from my medicine?
ask.a: Mainly if the dose is a little too high. A systematic review found these effects occur when TSH is pushed low; at the right dose they match placebo. Your August results hint your dose may have been high then. B12 is not a known cause.

We can't calculate it yet, and we won't guess. The validated method needs 9 blood results you haven't had: albumin, creatinine, fasting glucose, CRP, a blood count (4 values) and ALP. They're all in your panel, so you'll see it at your next assessment.

ask.q: Do I really need the antibody test?
ask.a: It's the most useful new test for you. It shows whether your hypothyroidism is autoimmune, which shapes how it's followed and what your family may want to know.

ask.q: What does my mood score mean?
ask.a: Your answers give mild scores for low mood and mild-to-moderate for worry. These are screening scores, not a diagnosis. Anxiety and low mood are more common in treated hypothyroidism, and you're already working with a therapist, which is the right support.

Book your personalised panel - ideally with your thyroid test around 16 January, fasting, in the morning, before your tablet. When the results arrive, every Mutanex analysis runs on them, your twin moves to version 2, and your doctor reviews a plan with you.

ask.q: Which vaccines or screening tests am I due?
ask.a: At 24, three things apply: a cervical screening test every 3 years, catch-up HPV vaccination until you turn 27 if you missed it, and a Tdap booster if you never had one. None is about your thyroid or back, which is why they are easy to miss.

ask.q: What exercise is best for my back?
ask.a: For long-term back pain, exercise helps and no single type is clearly better, so keep what you enjoy and can stick to. Your strength training and stretches fit. Standing breaks at work help too, and a physiotherapist can tailor a plan for the L4-L5 disc.

ask.q: Could sleep be making me tired?
ask.a: Possibly. Your bedtime moves between 22:30 and 01:00, and you said tiredness is worse after a poor night. Studies link poorer sleep with an underactive thyroid, though which causes which is not known. A steadier bedtime is a low-risk thing to try for a month.

Two things from your record: keep your tablet away from breakfast and fibre, and add vegetables and fruit, since you have 0 to 1 servings a day. Swapping sugary drinks for water most days also helps your heart and blood sugar over time.

ask.q: Which organs has my twin assessed?
ask.a: So far your thyroid, mind and mood, lower back and skin are assessed from your records and questionnaire; they are solid and coloured on your twin. Heart, kidneys, liver, pancreas, blood, lungs, digestion and reproductive health are ghosted until your panel measures them.

ask.q: Should I ask for T3 or a different thyroid medicine?
ask.a: Combination medicines have not been shown to be consistently better than levothyroxine alone. The first steps are steady tablet timing, the right dose and checking other causes of your symptoms. Discuss any change with your thyroid specialist.

glossary: TSH
Thyroid-stimulating hormone. Made by the pituitary gland; high means your body wants more thyroid hormone.
Free T4 / Free T3
The thyroid hormones in your blood that are available to your body.
Levothyroxine
Your thyroid medicine: a copy of the hormone T4.
Anti-TPO
An antibody that shows whether a thyroid condition is autoimmune.
PHQ-9 / GAD-7
Short questionnaires that screen for low mood and worry. Not a diagnosis.
HbA1c
Your average blood sugar over about 3 months.
ApoB and Lp(a)
Markers of the particles that carry cholesterol into artery walls; Lp(a) is inherited and measured once.
hs-CRP
A sensitive marker of background inflammation.
eGFR
An estimate of how well your kidneys filter blood.
Biological age
An estimate of how old your body seems from blood results, compared with your calendar age.
Evidence grade
How strong the research is: A strong, B good, C moderate, D early.
Digital twin
A model of your health built from your own records, which grows as new results arrive.

info_needed.why: Determines whether repeat imaging is warranted and whether current findings differ from baseline.

info_needed.item: How your back pain has changed over time
info_needed.why: Failure of conservative therapy is a trigger for imaging and specialist referral in the guidelines.

F9.statement: Nearly all spontaneous (presumed autoimmune) primary overt hypothyroidism is antibody-positive, and TPOAb is more often detectable than TgAb. A TPOAb result would therefore mainly confirm or refute an autoimmune etiology rather than redirect therapy.
F9.limitations: Etiologic classification is not the same as a management change. The data are from untreated or newly diagnosed patients in older studies and assays. TPOAb-negative autoimmune disease can occur because TgAb exists as an alternative marker.
F9.population: Adults with newly diagnosed primary overt hypothyroidism in a population cohort; older reference-style reviews

F26.statement: Autoimmune atrophic gastritis and celiac disease are the autoimmune conditions most specifically linked with autoimmune thyroiditis. They can present with anaemia, micronutrient deficiency and impaired absorption of oral drugs. Parietal cell antibodies were the most common organ-specific autoantibody in a large ATD cohort, followed by GADA.
F26.limitations: Mostly narrative review and prevalence data. Autoantibody prevalence is not the same as clinical disease. The sources do not show that antibody screening improves outcomes. The patient is much younger than the cohort and of South Asian ancestry.
F26.population: Adults with Hashimoto's thyroiditis or other autoimmune thyroid disease. The cohort was 1502 Italian patients, mostly women with a mean age of about 53.

Fatigue and sleepiness were not assessed. The mean age is older than the patient's and there is no South Asian-specific data. Only a narrow TSH range was included.
F15.population: Spanish primary-care women (mean age about 35) with primary hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine for at least 6 months and TSH 0.4-4.0 mIU/L, versus women without thyroid disease.

F10.statement: Biotin supplementation is a documented cause of analytical interference in streptavidin-biotin-based immunoassays, the formats commonly used for thyroid hormone measurement. It can produce false positive or false negative results and a seemingly coherent but spurious hormonal profile, including a false biochemical picture of hyperthyroidism.
F10.limitations: Narrative review abstract only. The excerpt gives no prevalence, no assay-by-assay susceptibility and no biotin intake thresholds. Whether a given TSH, FT4 or FT3 assay uses streptavidin-biotin chemistry is not stated for this patient.
F10.population: General patients undergoing immunoassay-based hormone testing; not specific to hypothyroidism or to this patient.

F11.statement: Thyroid function immunoassays (TSH, free T4, free T3) are vulnerable to six main interference types: macro-TSH, biotin, anti-streptavidin antibodies, anti-ruthenium antibodies, thyroid hormone autoantibodies and heterophilic antibodies. Reported interferences often led to misdiagnosis or inappropriate management. Suspicion should be raised when clinical and biochemical findings are discordant, and identification relies on additional laboratory work-up.
F11.limitations: Review of reported cases, so subject to reporting bias. The sources list no supplement other than biotin among the six interference types. Ashwagandha is not among them.
F11.population: Patients undergoing thyroid function testing; case-report-derived data (more than 150 patients).

F25.limitations: Trials were small and short (up to 12 months), and most symptom outcomes were low or very low certainty. The direction of the heart-rate difference is not specified in the excerpt.

F31.statement:
A descriptive review of major guidelines (Endocrine Society, ETA, RANZCOG, ATA, ACOG) found agreement on several points:
- Overt hypothyroidism should be treated during pregnancy and also before conception, with similar management and treatment targets.
- Universal screening is discouraged, and targeted TSH screening of high-risk patients is supported. The 2026 ATA guideline provides updated recommendations on thyroid function testing and hypothyroidism management across preconception, pregnancy and postpartum. Its specific recommendations were not in the supplied abstract.
F31.limitations: The ATA 2026 recommendation tables were not supplied. The guideline comparison is a descriptive narrative review. Exact surveillance intervals and targets cannot be extracted from these sources.
F31.population: Women with thyroid disease before, during and after pregnancy

F30.population: Adults with subclinical hypothyroidism versus healthy controls (8 studies; 2916 patients with subclinical hypothyroidism); treatment status not described in the abstract.

F12.population: Adults and mixed-age patients with thyroid disorders across 64 studies (n=28597); Asian and European subgroups differed.

F6.statement: A systematic review of 12 studies found that levothyroxine at replacement doses had a very low risk of cardiac, neuropsychiatric and musculoskeletal adverse events. Adverse events occurred mainly when TSH was suppressed, and blinded placebo-controlled trials in euthyroid patients showed no significant differences. Some subjective symptoms may be placebo or nocebo effects.
F6.limitations: Only 12 heterogeneous studies; most comparisons were underpowered with wide confidence intervals. Several RCTs were unregistered. Anxiety was one of several pooled neuropsychiatric outcomes. The excerpt does not show anxiety-specific results. Not specific to a young woman of South Asian ancestry.
F6.population: Mostly adults with hypothyroidism or subclinical hypothyroidism (mean ages 14-93 years across studies). The review's most explicit anxiety data come from studies of suppressive or supraphysiologic dosing. Anxiety was one of many outcomes.

F7.statement: A systematic review found that adverse events attributed to levothyroxine, including neuropsychiatric events such as headache, occurred mainly when TSH was suppressed. In euthyroid patients in blinded placebo-controlled trials there was no significant difference. The pattern suggests thyroid status (over-replacement versus normal TSH) is the main discriminator for a drug-related headache.
F7.limitations: Small, heterogeneous studies. Headache-specific results are in sections not shown in the excerpt. Mostly not powered for headache. Findings are associations, and the excerpt does not show whether headache itself differed by group.
F7.population: Mixed populations (12 studies, n=1817), mostly hypothyroid or subclinical hypothyroid patients, plus patients on TSH-suppressive therapy.

F14.statement: Hypothyroidism can plausibly account for fatigue and dry skin, but its symptoms are non-specific. No single symptom reliably identifies thyroid disease, and persistent symptoms in levothyroxine-treated patients are hard to attribute to thyroid status. This supports checking whether current thyroid replacement is biochemically adequate while keeping non-thyroid causes open.
F14.limitations: The review is narrative. The case-control study addressed untreated, newly diagnosed overt disease, not treated patients. The sources do not address a 24-year-old woman on stable levothyroxine.
F14.population: Adults with overt or subclinical hypothyroidism; population-based case-control study of newly diagnosed overt autoimmune hypothyroidism

F18.statement: A small double-blind placebo-controlled RCT of intramuscular B12 in chronic mechanical low back pain or sciatic neuritis found a statistically significant between-group advantage for active treatment on pain (VAS) and disability, and less paracetamol use. Both groups improved sharply, and the participants had no signs of nutritional deficiency.
F18.limitations: Small, published in 2000, one agent and regimen. The large placebo-arm improvement suggests a strong non-specific response. Only the abstract was available, so risk of bias is unclear.

F19.statement: A phase 3 RCT of injectable hydroxocobalamin + thiamine + pyridoxine added to NSAIDs in chronic mechanical low back pain showed a higher proportion with ≥30% NRS reduction at day 28 than placebo + NSAIDs. Adverse events were more frequent with treatment, with no significant difference in serious events. The effect cannot be attributed to B12 alone.
F19.limitations: Combination product (B1/B6/B12) with concurrent NSAIDs, so the B12 contribution cannot be isolated. Short follow-up (28 days). Only the abstract was seen. Higher adverse-event incidence in the treatment arm.

F23.statement: Motor control exercise (MCE) is not clinically more effective than other forms of exercise for chronic non-specific LBP at any follow-up period (including long-term, 12 months or more). Choice of exercise may therefore reasonably depend on preference, training, cost and safety rather than on exercise type.
F23.limitations: Non-specific LBP population; the patient has a confirmed L4-L5 disc compression, and applicability to disc-related pain is indirect. Quality ranged from low to high depending on comparison. Exercise dosing is not given in the abstract.

F4.statement: The only RCT of ashwagandha on thyroid indices (50 adults with subclinical hypothyroidism, 600 mg/day for 8 weeks) reported significantly improved TSH, T3 and T4 versus placebo. Ashwagandha can therefore shift thyroid function tests in people with a mild hypothyroid state. Participants were not described as taking levothyroxine, so the result cannot be extrapolated directly to treated hypothyroidism.
F4.limitations: Small pilot (n=50), 8 weeks, single centre, no stratification by sex, levothyroxine-treated patients not studied, autoimmune status not reported in the abstract, industry-style standardised extract may not match this patient's product.
